annotationRationale: The essential task is to count intersections using range, signs, periodicity, existence, and uniqueness. Both sources use the same counting route. The solution supplies the necessary uniqueness proof using explicitly derived elementary graph properties.

classificationReview.areaCheck: Algebra is appropriate for this function-intersection problem.

review.questionCheck: Solutions lie in [1/20,20]. Ten negative arches contribute 20 roots, and 190 positive arches contribute 380 roots when x = 1 is included. That endpoint is shared, giving 399 distinct roots, choice D. The supplied figures are schematic and consistent with this count; the candidate supplies the uniqueness proof that the pictures alone cannot establish.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: No sharedQuestions methods were supplied. LIVE's lobe count and Random Math's period count are merged into one equivalent route. The candidate replaces LIVE's calculus justification and Random Math's visual assertion with an elementary uniqueness proof. No genuinely different accessible supplied route is omitted.
review.annotationCheck: Function zeros, sinusoidal period, and logarithmic properties are correctly assessed. Sine range, monotonicity, angle identities, and AM-GM are appropriate support nodes. The new chord properties are introduced and derived rather than attributed to an unrelated broad node.
review.areaCheck: Algebra is appropriate for this function-intersection problem.

methodReviews.mathCheck: All arch ranges and endpoint signs are correct. Strict convexity gives exactly two roots on each negative arch. Falling positive halves have exactly one root by monotonicity. On a rising half, two roots would satisfy a logarithm secant slope below 1, while the bound L(v) < 1999/2000 gives cos(phi) > 1/40 and hence a sine secant slope above 1, a contradiction. The shared root x = 1 is subtracted exactly once, giving 399.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Both cited sources support the arch-counting framework. The elementary chord-and-secant uniqueness argument is a substantial original completion, accurately described as source-informed-original. Neither source is incorrectly presented as an official MAA solution.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The proof explains why signs select the arches and why existence alone is insufficient. Concavity is defined and established using AM-GM and a sine identity; the secant comparisons then provide a complete noncalculus uniqueness argument. The table summarizes justified counts and handles the shared endpoint correctly.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: All seven IDs have direct roles. The sine identities are elementary consequences of the mapped angle formulas; concavity and the required secant bounds are developed in the explanation, so no unsupported advanced technique is being substituted for an exact concept.
